assignments.title: Quick Write 1 — My Hero
assignments.html:
PURPOSE: Write an early draft of what a hero is, drawn from personal experience and thinking rather than the text, as the first scaffold toward the module project.

Steps

  1. Choose someone, real or fictional, regarded as a hero. The person does not have to be famous.
  2. Write 2–3 paragraphs (about 150–200 words) that answer three questions: who the person is and what they did, with enough detail for a stranger to understand; what makes them a hero, naming at least one specific quality or action; and whether they ever broke a rule, disobeyed an authority, or did something others disagreed with, and whether that made them more or less heroic.

assignments.title: Mini-Research Task — Is There a Historical Robin Hood?
assignments.html:
PURPOSE: Research whether a real person stands behind the Robin Hood legend and report how reliable sources answer the question.

Steps

  1. Find two reliable sources that discuss whether a historical Robin Hood existed: an encyclopedia article (for example, Britannica), a museum or university website, or a library database article. A random blog, forum post, fan wiki, or AI chatbot answer is not reliable. Ask the teacher when unsure.
  2. Take brief notes on each source: what it says about whether Robin Hood was real, and what evidence or reasoning it gives.
  3. In Microsoft Word, write a short paragraph (5–8 sentences) stating what the two sources agree on and where they disagree.
  4. Name each source inside the paragraph as it is used (According to Britannica, or The Nottingham Castle Museum says…).
  5. In the same paragraph, explain in own words why historians and scholars might still disagree about whether a legendary figure was a real person.
  6. Add a Sources list at the bottom, one entry per source, in the MLA web-page pattern below, and submit.

Requirements

  • Two sources that fit the reliable-source description above.
  • Both sources named in the paragraph.
  • MLA pattern for each Sources entry, in this order and with this punctuation: Author or Organization. "Title of the Article." Name of the Website, URL.
  • Example entry: Encyclopaedia Britannica. "Robin Hood." Britannica Kids, https://kids.britannica.com/kids/article/Robin-Hood/353686.
  • A page with no author begins with the organization that publishes the site.

Submit

  • File name: LastName_FirstName_MiniResearch_ELA6
  • Word document (.docx) saved to the ELA6 OneDrive folder and submitted through the Microsoft OneDrive tab.

Done when

  • I used two sources that fit the reliable-source description.
  • My paragraph names both sources and states clearly what they agree or disagree on.
  • I explained in my own words why sources might disagree about a legendary figure.
  • My Sources list has an entry for each source in the MLA pattern.
  • My file is named correctly, saved to the ELA6 OneDrive folder, and submitted through the OneDrive tab.

assignments.title: Module Project — The Power of Choice: Daniel's Journey
assignments.html:
PURPOSE: Write a 4–5 paragraph expository and argumentative essay titled "The Power of Choice: Daniel's Journey" that traces Daniel's change from hatred and vengeance toward love and argues what his choices prove about the novel's claim that love can do what hatred cannot.

"Can love accomplish what hatred cannot? Use The Bronze Bow to argue your position."

Steps

  1. Week 4: Use Quick Write 4 (thesis, three pieces of evidence, objection) as the planning draft. Save the essay file as LastName_FirstName_PowerOfChoice_ELA6_Draft1 in OneDrive → Optima → ELA → ELA6 and expand the plan into a full draft.
  2. Write the five parts listed under Requirements, using the three ways writers persuade and naming them as they are used: logos (sound reasoning: a clear claim, evidence, and explanation that holds together), ethos (trust, earned by stating the other side fairly and handling evidence honestly), and pathos (the real, specific moments from Daniel's story that move a reader).
  3. Add the craft items listed under Requirements and underline each where it appears.
  4. Week 5: Revise Draft1 into the full five-part essay with Review → Track Changes on. Save each clean revision after self-review or feedback as LastName_FirstName_PowerOfChoice_ELA6_Final. Never overwrite a draft; keep every version. (Word in OneDrive keeps a Version History under File → Info → Version History.)
  5. Check the M365 items below, then submit the _Final Word document.

Requirements

  • Opening — thesis. An arguable claim that says both what is believed and why; the paragraph ends by setting up the argument (logos).
  • The other side — stated fairly. The strongest honest case against the thesis, using Daniel's real experience (for example, that hatred kept him alive and fighting). Stating the opposition fairly is ethos.
  • Central argument. Turn the conversation ("And yet…") and state the strongest claim, grounded in the novel.
  • Evidence. At least three specific moments named by chapter, each with commentary on why it proves the claim, not just what it shows. Specific, true scenes carry pathos as well as logos.
  • Answer and close. Show why the argument holds even granting the other side's strongest point, then restate the thesis with force.
  • At least 5 vocabulary words from across the module (e.g., zealot, vendetta, contempt, compassion, perceive, allegiance, betrayal, reconciliation, redemption), used naturally and underlined.
  • At least one periodic sentence (main clause withheld to the end), marked "PS" in the margin, and underlined.
  • At least one participial phrase, marked "PP" in the margin, and underlined.
  • Parallel structure where Rosh's view is set against Jesus' view.
  • An MLA Works Cited line: Speare, Elizabeth George. The Bronze Bow. Houghton Mifflin, 1961.
  • One Word document; title in Heading 1 style; body in Times New Roman 12 or Calibri 11.
  • M365 skill practiced: drafting and revising a multi-draft document with Heading styles, Track Changes, and Version History (Word — MOS Core).

assignments.title: Module Project — "What Lasts"
assignments.html:
PURPOSE: Argue that one of four themes connects at least three characters from three different texts read this year, and record a short oral reflection; the essay and recording are submitted together.

Steps

  1. Choose one theme and three characters from three different texts. Suggested characters (others are allowed if the case can be made): Heroism: St. George, Robin Hood, King Arthur, Benedick. Self-Sacrifice: Daniel, Lancelot and Guinevere, Prospero, Hero. Happiness: Midas, Beatrice and Benedick, Miranda, Daniel. Duty: St. George, King Arthur, Joel, Hero.
  2. Open with a topic sentence that states the argument. Model: "Across three very different stories, heroism takes the same shape: a person faces something that could destroy them and moves toward it anyway, not because they are unafraid, but because the call in front of them matters more than their fear."
  3. Give evidence from each of the three characters: the specific moment that supports the argument, not a general trait, with a transition between characters (likewise, in contrast, similarly, while).
  4. Write one sentence naming what all three share, beginning "What all three of these characters share is …".
  5. Close with a sentence on what the theme means as an idea and why literature keeps returning to it. A periodic sentence works well here (see the Week 3 grammar lesson).
  6. Record a 2–3 minute oral reflection ("What I Carry Forward") answering: "What is one thing you are carrying forward from this year's reading, and which character helped you see it?" Name the thing, describe the character, and say why it matters now. The character need not match the essay.

Requirements

  • Essay of 200–250 words in Word, title in Heading 1, body in Times New Roman 12 or Calibri 11.
  • Three characters from three different texts; two characters from the same play count as one text.
  • Central questions: Heroism, what does it look like to do the right thing when it costs something; Self-Sacrifice, what does a person give up and receive in return; Happiness, how do the characters discover what happiness requires; Duty, what does a person owe, to whom, and what happens when it is paid.

Answer these five out loud, in order. Notes in front of you are fine; a script read word for word is not.
›What is the book, and how far did you get?
›Pick one character. What do they want, and what is in the way?
›Describe a moment where that character makes a choice you would not have made. Why did they make it?
›Read one sentence or short passage you marked, and say why that one.
›Who should read this book, and who should skip it?
2Dramatic ReadingABOUT 3 MINUTES
›Choose a passage of roughly 150 to 300 words where a character is under pressure: deciding, arguing, afraid, or hiding something.
›Read it aloud as that character. Decide before you record what they want in this moment, then let your pace, volume and pauses show it.
›Then talk for about a minute: who is this character, what do they want here, and what did you do with your voice to show it? Name one specific choice you made.
3Make the CaseABOUT 3 MINUTES
You are a guest on a books podcast and the host has given you three minutes to make one argument. House rule of the show: you have to take the side most listeners will not.
›Name what you are arguing about, and say where it falls in the book. Pick something people genuinely disagree over: a moral dilemma, a turn nobody saw coming, or a decision a character made that readers still argue about.
›Take the unpopular side and say it in your first sentence. If most readers think the character was right, argue that they were wrong. If nobody could disagree with your claim, it is not an argument yet.
›Give two pieces of evidence from the text: a line, a scene, something a character says or does. Say roughly where each one falls.
›Answer the strongest objection, the one the host would come back at you with. State it fairly first, then answer it.
›Land it. Finish with one sentence a listener would still be turning over after the episode ends.
4A Different EndingABOUT 3 MINUTES
Only take this one if you finished the book. You are going to replace the ending, and you cannot rewrite an ending you never got to.
›Say how the book actually ends, in two or three sentences. Be accurate. The rest of this only works if your listener knows what you are changing.
›Name the exact point where your version branches off, then describe your ending in detail. What happens, who it happens to, and how does it finish?
›Explain why yours is better for this book. Not happier, and not kinder to your favourite character, but truer to what the story has been about. Name the idea or theme you are serving.
›Say what your ending costs. Every ending gives something up. Name what is lost by not keeping the one the author wrote.
Full credit
 
☐Clear evidence the book was read.
☐Points at a specific moment or line, not the story in general.
☐Says something original: a judgement, a disagreement, a question.
☐Audible the whole way through.

quizzes.title: Module 4 Intro — Robin Hood: Portrait of a Hero
quizzes.description:
📋 Before we begin

Module 4: Robin Hood — Portrait of a Hero. Over eight weeks, the class reads Roger Lancelyn Green's retelling of one of the oldest hero stories in the English-speaking world, following Robin Hood from his first days as an outlaw in Sherwood Forest, through his encounters with the Sheriff of Nottingham, to King Richard himself. One question runs through all eight weeks:

What makes a true hero — and what happens when justice and law are not the same thing?

The module project is a "Portrait of a Hero": an analytical essay, built in Microsoft Word across Weeks 5–7, that argues with evidence from the text whether Robin Hood is a true hero.

This short reflection survey has no right or wrong answers. Responses show the teacher where the class is starting. Answer honestly.

Reading access & copyright. Students must obtain lawful access to the assigned literary work separately. Optima course materials are original instructional materials designed to support analysis, discussion, and assessment of the work. Copyrighted text, images, illustrations, panels, audio, or other protected materials are not reproduced in Canvas, videos, downloadable files, or teacher resources except where expressly licensed, in the public domain, or approved as a limited fair-use excerpt for instructional analysis.

The Adventures of Robin Hood is read from the student's own copy of the book.

questions.text:
Here is the essential question for this module:

"What makes a true hero — and what happens when justice and law are not the same thing?"

Write 2–3 sentences giving your first, honest answer. You will return to this question at the end of the module. Do not research an answer — just write what you think right now.
Which best describes what you already know about Robin Hood?

answers.text: I've heard the name but don't know much about him.
I've seen a movie or TV show about Robin Hood.
I've read a book or story about Robin Hood before.
I know a lot about Robin Hood — the legend, the history, or both.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes how you think about justice right now?

answers.text: Justice means following the law, no matter what.
Justice means doing what is right, even if the law disagrees.
Justice and the law are usually the same thing.
I'm not sure yet — I want to think about this more.

questions.text: Look at the module project description above. In one sentence, describe what you think the hardest part of the "Portrait of a Hero" essay will be for you.
How confident are you with reading-comprehension quizzes right now?

answers.text: Very confident — I usually do well on reading quizzes.
Somewhat confident — I do okay but sometimes miss things.
Not very confident — I find comprehension quizzes difficult.

quizzes.title: Grammar Quiz — Proper & Common Nouns

questions.text: Which of these is a proper noun?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — Sherwood Forest names one specific place, so it is a proper noun and takes capitals.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A proper noun names one specific, particular thing by its own name. Which choice does that?

questions.text: A common noun is best described as —

answers.text: a word that always takes a capital letter
a word that names any member of a group
the name of one specific person
a word that shows an action

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a common noun (sheriff, town, king) names any member of a group and stays lowercase.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A common noun names a kind of thing, not one specific named thing. The specific-name kind is a proper noun.

questions.text: In "the cruel sheriff hunted the poor folk," which word is a common noun?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — sheriff names a kind of officer here, not one named person, so it is a common noun.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Cruel" and "poor" describe; "hunted" is an action. Which word names a kind of person?

questions.text: Which sentence capitalizes the proper noun correctly?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — the specific name Prince John is capitalized, and the plain words stay lowercase.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Capitalize the name (Prince John) and only the name. Do not lowercase the name or capitalize ordinary words.

questions.text: Which list contains only proper nouns?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — Nottingham, King Richard, and England each name one specific place or person.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Every word in the list must name one specific person or place. Some of these are general kinds of things.

quizzes.title: Vocabulary Quiz — Words of an Unjust World

questions.text: The Saxon poor are treated as mere serfs, bound to till the land for their lords. A serf is —

answers.text: a poor peasant bound to work a lord's land

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a serf is a poor peasant bound to a lord's land, with almost no rights.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A serf is the lowest, bound rank of the poor — not a free farmer or an officer.

questions.text: Robin is falsely accused of treason. Treason means —

answers.text: the crime of betraying your king or country

questions.feedback_correct: Right — treason is betraying your king or country; the charge against Robin is a lie.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Treason is a crime of betrayal against the king or country, not an object or a contest.

questions.text: Green calls Prince John a usurper. A usurper is —

answers.text: someone who seizes power that is not rightfully theirs
a loyal servant of the king

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a usurper grabs power he has no right to; Prince John seizes the throne while Richard lives.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A usurper takes power unjustly. A loyal servant or a poor farmer is the opposite idea.

questions.text: The Sheriff's soldiers wore his livery as they closed in. Livery means —

answers.text: the uniform or colors that show whose servant a man is

questions.feedback_correct: Right — livery is the colors or uniform a lord's men wear so you know whom they serve.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Livery is clothing that marks whose man a soldier is, not a weapon or a place.

questions.text: Which sentence uses yeoman correctly?

answers.text: "The king signed the yeoman into law."
"She wore a yeoman of white silk."
"The free yeoman farmed his own small plot of land."
"They sharpened the yeoman before the battle."

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a yeoman is a free man who farms his own land, ranking above a serf.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A yeoman is a person — a free small farmer — not a law, a cloth, or a weapon.

quizzes.title: Grammar Quiz — Simple & Compound Sentences

questions.text: What kind of sentence is "The outlaws wore Lincoln green"?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — this is one complete thought with a single subject and verb, so it is a simple sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Could you split this into two sentences that each stand alone? You cannot, so it is simple.

questions.text: A compound sentence is —

answers.text: two complete thoughts joined by a comma and a joining word

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a compound sentence joins two complete thoughts with a comma plus a word like and, but, or, so.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A compound sentence joins two thoughts that could each stand alone. One thought alone is a simple sentence.

questions.text: Which of these is a correct compound sentence?

answers.text: Robin lost the fight, but he welcomed the winner.
Robin lost the fight he welcomed the winner.
Robin lost the fight, he welcomed the winner.
Losing the fight on the bridge.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — two complete thoughts joined by a comma and but. That is a correct compound sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A compound sentence needs a comma AND a joining word. Choices with only a comma or no joining word are run-ons; one choice is not even a full sentence.

questions.text: Which choice correctly fixes the run-on "The bridge was narrow neither man would yield"?

answers.text: The bridge was narrow neither man would yield.
The bridge was narrow, neither man would yield.
The bridge was narrow, so neither man would yield.
The bridge was narrow so neither man would yield.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a comma plus the joining word so correctly joins the two complete thoughts.
questions.feedback_incorrect: To fix this run-on you need BOTH a comma and a joining word (so). A comma alone, or a joining word with no comma, does not fix it.

questions.text: Which word is a joining word (coordinating conjunction) that can build a compound sentence?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — and (with but, or, so, for, nor, yet) joins two complete thoughts into a compound sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A joining word connects two complete thoughts. "Quickly," "forest," and "brave" describe or name; they do not join.

quizzes.title: Vocabulary Quiz — Words of the Greenwood

questions.text: Stripped of his lands, Robin becomes an outlaw. An outlaw is —

answers.text: a person placed outside the protection of the law

questions.feedback_correct: Right — an outlaw is placed outside the law's protection; the law brands Robin one, but his band wears the name with pride.
questions.feedback_incorrect: An outlaw is a person outside the law's protection, not an officer, a weapon, or a pilgrim.

questions.text: On the bridge, Robin and the stranger fight with the quarter-staff. A quarter-staff is —

answers.text: a long wooden pole used as a weapon

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a quarter-staff is a long, stout fighting pole gripped with both hands.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A quarter-staff is a wooden fighting pole, not an animal, a cloth, or a place.

questions.text: The Sheriff's men demand a harsh tithe from the poor. A tithe is —

answers.text: a tenth part taken as a payment or fine

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a tithe is a tenth taken as a payment or fine, here squeezed from Robin's old tenants.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A tithe is a tenth taken from people, not a feast, a place, or a symbol.

questions.text: Robin says King Richard is his true liege lord. A liege lord is —

answers.text: a lord or king a person owes loyalty to

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a liege lord is the lord or king you owe loyalty to; Robin stays loyal to Richard, not Prince John.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A liege lord is one you owe loyalty to, not an enemy, a merchant, or a servant.

questions.text: Which sentence uses renounce correctly?

answers.text: "She renounced the arrow at the target."
"To stay safe, Lord Fitzwalter chose to renounce Robin and side with the prince."
"He renounced his bow until it was sharp."
"They renounced across the bridge in single file."

questions.feedback_correct: Right — to renounce someone is to give them up or formally reject them, as Fitzwalter does to Robin.
questions.feedback_incorrect: To renounce is to reject or give up something. It is not aiming, sharpening, or crossing.

quizzes.title: Grammar Quiz — Subject–Verb Agreement

questions.text: Choose the verb that agrees with the subject: "The outlaws ______ Lincoln green in the forest."
questions.feedback_correct: Right — outlaws is plural, so the plural verb wear agrees.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Count the subject. Outlaws is plural, so the verb must be plural: wear.

questions.text: Choose the verb that agrees: "The leader of the outlaws ______ brave and fair."
questions.feedback_correct: Right — cross out of the outlaws; the subject is the singular leader, so the verb is is.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The phrase of the outlaws is not the subject. The true subject is the singular leader.

questions.text: Which word is the true subject of this sentence? "The band of merry men lives in Sherwood."
questions.feedback_correct: Right — band is the subject. Of merry men is a phrase that describes it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The verb's subject is band, a collective noun. Of merry men just describes the band.

questions.text: Choose the verb that agrees: "Robin's band ______ in the greenwood each morning."
questions.feedback_correct: Right — band is a collective noun naming one group, so it takes the singular meets.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A collective noun like band names one unit, so it usually takes a singular verb: meets.

questions.text: Which sentence has correct subject–verb agreement?

answers.text: Friar Tuck join the band after the fight.
The honest yeomen works their own land and pays no fine.
Little John and Will Scarlet guard the camp at night.
Marian, along with the foresters, shoot at the festival.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — Little John and Will Scarlet is a compound (plural) subject, so the plural verb guard agrees.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check each subject. Friar Tuck needs joins; yeomen needs work; in D the subject is the singular Marian, so it needs shoots. Only C agrees.

quizzes.title: Vocabulary Quiz — Words of the Greenwood

questions.text: "I beg one last boon of you," said the knight. A boon is —

answers.text: a favor that is asked for or granted

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a boon is a favor asked or granted; the knight begs one last favor.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A boon is something requested or given, not a weapon or a place.

questions.text: Robin spares the honest yeoman who works his own small field. A yeoman is —

answers.text: a free man who farms his own land

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a yeoman is a free man who farms his own land, below a noble but above a serf.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A yeoman is neither a churchman nor a noble; he is a free, land-working man.

questions.text: Friar Tuck lived as a hermit by the river before joining the band. A hermit is —

answers.text: a person who lives alone, often for religious reasons
a soldier in the Sheriff's pay

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a hermit lives alone, often for religious reasons; that is how Tuck lives at first.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A hermit is someone who lives alone, not a soldier, a tool, or a contest.

questions.text: Which sentence uses quarter-staff correctly?

answers.text: "She wore a fine quarter-staff of white silk."
"The abbot signed the quarter-staff to seize the land."
"They built a quarter-staff by the river to live in."
"Little John fought Robin with a quarter-staff on the narrow bridge."

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a quarter-staff is a long wooden pole used as a weapon, gripped with both hands.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A quarter-staff is a wooden weapon, not clothing, a document, or a dwelling.

questions.text: The outlaws made their home in the greenwood. Greenwood most nearly means —

answers.text: the green forest, the outlaws' refuge

questions.feedback_correct: Right — the greenwood is the green forest, the band's home and refuge.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The greenwood is the forest where the band lives, not a castle, abbey, or town.

quizzes.title: Grammar Quiz — Verb-Tense Consistency

questions.text: Which sentence has an unnecessary tense shift?

answers.text: Robin disguises himself and rides into Nottingham.
Robin disguised himself and rode into Nottingham.
Robin disguises himself and rode into Nottingham.
Robin will disguise himself and will ride into Nottingham.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — disguises is present and rode is past, so the tense jumps for no reason.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Compare the two verbs. In C, one is present and one is past in a single action — that is the unnecessary shift.

questions.text: When you write about a story, the standard tense is the present. Choose the correct verb: "In Chapter 11, Robin ______ the Sheriff with a clever trade."
questions.feedback_correct: Right — to discuss what happens in a book, use the present tense: fools.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Writing about a story uses the present tense. We say Robin fools the Sheriff.

questions.text: Which sentence changes tense for a good reason (a real change in time)?

answers.text: Robin won the arrow yesterday, and today he plans his next trick.
Robin enters the town and slipped away unseen.
The Sheriff schemes and lost the bargain at once.
Marian shoots at the festival and outshot the foresters.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — yesterday and today are different times, so the tense change is meaningful and correct.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A tense change is fine only when the time truly changes. A names two different times; the others jump for no reason.

questions.text: Which sentence is consistent in tense?

answers.text: Robin fooled the Sheriff and escapes the town.
Robin fools the Sheriff and escapes the town.
Robin fools the Sheriff and escaped the town.
Robin will fool the Sheriff and escaped the town.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — both verbs are present (fools, escapes), so the sentence stays consistent.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check that both verbs share one tense. Only B keeps both in the present.

questions.text: A classmate writes: "Robin entered the contest and wins the silver arrow." What is the best fix?

answers.text: Make both verbs match: "Robin enters the contest and wins the silver arrow."
Add the word yesterday to the front.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — entered (past) and wins (present) clash; matching them to the present fixes the shift.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The two verbs are in different tenses for no reason. Make them match (both present, or both past) to fix it.

quizzes.title: Vocabulary Quiz — Words of the Contest

questions.text: The outlaws roasted venison over the fire. Venison is —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — venison is deer meat; hunting the King's deer was against the law.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Venison is a food — the meat of a deer — not a weapon or an announcement.

questions.text: Robin slid the silver arrow into his quiver. A quiver is —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — a quiver holds arrows; Robin drops his prize arrow into it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A quiver is the case that carries arrows, not clothing, a place, or a person.

questions.text: Prince John ordered heralds to proclaim a great archery contest. To proclaim is to —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — to proclaim is to announce something officially and in public, as Prince John does.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Proclaim means to announce publicly and officially — the opposite of hiding or canceling.

questions.text: "Come, sirrah, pay up at once!" Used this way, sirrah is —

answers.text: a sharp, scornful way to address a man

questions.feedback_correct: Right — sirrah is an old, sharp way to address a man, often showing scorn or command.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Sirrah is not friendly; it is a sharp, commanding way to speak to someone.

questions.text: Which sentence uses disguise correctly?

answers.text: "He drew the disguise from his quiver and shot."
"In a butcher's disguise, Robin entered Nottingham unrecognized."
"They roasted the disguise over the fire."
"The herald rode out to disguise the contest to the land."

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a disguise is a change of appearance that hides who you are, exactly what Robin uses.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A disguise hides your identity. It is not an arrow, a food, or a way to announce something.

quizzes.title: Grammar Quiz — Complex Sentences

questions.text: Which group of words is a dependent clause (it cannot stand alone)?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — the starter word because leaves it hanging, so it cannot stand alone.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A dependent clause begins with a word like because, when, although. Which choice leaves you waiting for more?

questions.text: An independent clause is a group of words that —

answers.text: can stand on its own as a complete sentence

questions.feedback_correct: Right — an independent clause has a subject and verb and forms a full sentence by itself.
questions.feedback_incorrect: An independent clause is complete on its own. Words like because mark the dependent kind.

questions.text: Which sentence places the comma correctly?

answers.text: When Robin arrived the wedding had begun.
Robin arrived, when the wedding had begun.
When Robin arrived, the wedding had begun.
When Robin arrived the wedding, had begun.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — when the dependent clause comes first, a comma follows it before the independent clause.
questions.feedback_incorrect: If the because/when/although part comes first, put a comma after it. Which choice does that?

questions.text: Which one is a complex sentence (an independent clause joined to a dependent clause)?

answers.text: Robin disguised himself. He entered the church.
Robin disguised himself, and he entered the church.
Robin disguised himself because his enemies held the town.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a full sentence joined to a because clause makes one complex sentence that shows a reason.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A complex sentence joins one idea that can stand alone to one that cannot (a because/when/although part).

questions.text: In "Although Little John was jealous, he stayed loyal to Robin," which part is the dependent clause?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — although makes that part lean on the rest; it cannot stand alone.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The dependent clause is the part that cannot stand by itself. Which part begins with although?

quizzes.title: Vocabulary Quiz — Words of Disguise and the Road

questions.text: Little John put on a beggar's rags as a disguise. A disguise is —

answers.text: a changed appearance that hides who you are

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a disguise hides who you really are; Little John uses one to slip into Nottingham.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A disguise is about hiding your identity, not a song, a weapon, or a horse.

questions.text: Allin-a-Dale, a sad minstrel, played a sorrowful tune. A minstrel is —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — a minstrel is a wandering singer and musician; Allin-a-Dale is heartbroken in song.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A minstrel makes music and sings; the leather worker is a tanner.

questions.text: Robin and the tanner traded blows with a quarter-staff. A quarter-staff is —

answers.text: a long, two-handed wooden fighting pole

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a quarter-staff is the long wooden pole the two men fight with on the road.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A quarter-staff is a weapon, not a cloth, a beggar, or a horse.

questions.text: Arthur-a-Bland worked as a tanner. A tanner is a person who —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — a tanner makes leather from hides; that is Arthur-a-Bland's trade.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A tanner works leather. The singer is a minstrel.

questions.text: Which sentence uses jest correctly?

answers.text: "He rode his jest down the forest path."
"The band bearded the Sheriff half in jest, laughing as they fooled him."
"She wore a jest of fine green cloth."
"He sharpened his jest before the fight."

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a jest is a joke or playful trick; the band fools the Sheriff partly for fun.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A jest is a joke or playful trick, not a horse, a cloth, or a weapon.

quizzes.title: Grammar Quiz — Appositives

questions.text: An appositive is a noun or noun phrase that —

answers.text: renames the noun right next to it

questions.feedback_correct: Right — an appositive renames or explains the noun beside it (the Bishop, a corrupt churchman).
questions.feedback_incorrect: An appositive renames a noun; it does not show action or join sentences.

questions.text: In "The Bishop, a corrupt churchman, hunted Robin," which part is the appositive?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — a corrupt churchman renames the Bishop and tells you about him.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The appositive is the part that renames the noun Bishop. Which phrase does that?

questions.text: Which sentence sets off the middle appositive correctly?

answers.text: George-a-Greene the pinner of Wakefield joined the band.
George-a-Greene, the pinner of Wakefield joined the band.
George-a-Greene the pinner of Wakefield, joined the band.
George-a-Greene, the pinner of Wakefield, joined the band.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a middle appositive takes a comma before and a comma after.
questions.feedback_incorrect: When the appositive sits in the middle, surround it with two commas, one on each side.

questions.text: Which sentence punctuates the end appositive correctly?

answers.text: Robin trusted Little John, his tallest man.
Robin trusted Little John his tallest man.
Robin, trusted Little John his tallest man.
Robin trusted, Little John his tallest man.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — an appositive at the end of a sentence needs just one comma, placed before it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: When the appositive ends the sentence, put a single comma before it.

questions.text: In "Allin-a-Dale, a minstrel, sang for Robin," the appositive renames —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — a minstrel renames Allin-a-Dale, telling you who he is.
questions.feedback_incorrect: An appositive renames the noun right before it. Who is being called "a minstrel"?

quizzes.title: Vocabulary Quiz — Words of Pursuit and Peril

questions.text: Robin captured the Bishop and held him for ransom. A ransom is —

answers.text: money demanded to free a captive

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a ransom is payment demanded to free a captive; Robin demands it from the Bishop.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A ransom is about paying to free a captive, not a storm, an officer, or an attack.

questions.text: The Bishop set an ambush to catch Robin. An ambush is —

answers.text: a surprise attack from a hidden position

questions.feedback_correct: Right — an ambush is a surprise attack from hiding; Robin escapes it by disguise.
questions.feedback_incorrect: An ambush is a hidden, surprise attack, not a feast or a service.

questions.text: Worman, who once served Robin, is now called a traitor. A traitor is a person who —

answers.text: betrays a trust or a side

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a traitor betrays a trust; Worman broke his loyalty to Robin.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A traitor betrays those who trusted him. The animal-keeper is a pinner.

questions.text: Sir Guy of Gisborne is Robin's sworn enemy. Sworn here means —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — sworn means bound by an oath; Sir Guy has vowed to hunt Robin down.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Sworn means bound by a vow, not wealthy or friendly.

questions.text: Which sentence uses peril correctly?

answers.text: "He cooked the peril over the fire."
"As his enemies closed in, Robin was in great peril."
"She wore a peril of green silk."

questions.feedback_correct: Right — peril means serious, immediate danger; Robin's enemies put him in peril.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Peril is danger, not food, clothing, or a person.

quizzes.title: Grammar Quiz — Quoting & Citing Evidence

questions.text: A signal phrase is —

answers.text: a short introduction that names the source before a quote
the quotation marks around a quote
the last sentence of a paragraph

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a signal phrase (such as Green writes,) introduces a quote and names its source.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A signal phrase is the lead-in that names who is being quoted, not the marks or the page number.

questions.text: Which sentence introduces and punctuates the quotation correctly?

answers.text: Robin was just "he robbed only the corrupt".
"He robbed only the corrupt" Green writes.
Green writes that Robin "robbed only the corrupt."
Robin robbed only the corrupt Green writes.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — the signal phrase introduces the quote and the period sits inside the closing quotation mark.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The quote needs a signal phrase, and in American style the period goes inside the closing quotation mark.

questions.text: Which shows a correct parenthetical citation at the end of a sentence?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — the page number goes in parentheses after the closing quotation mark, and the period comes after the parenthesis.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Place the page number in parentheses after the closing quotation mark, then end with the period.

questions.text: What makes a quotation a "dropped quote"?

answers.text: It is longer than one line
It comes from the end of the book
It has no signal phrase and no citation

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a dropped quote appears with no lead-in and no citation, so the reader cannot tell who said it or check it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The problem with a dropped quote is that it is not introduced or cited, not its length or its source.

questions.text: Why does your essay add a page number after a quotation?

answers.text: So a reader can find the quote in the book and check it
Because every sentence needs a number

questions.feedback_correct: Right — the citation lets a reader open the same book and verify your evidence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The page number is there so a reader can locate and check the quote, not for length and not instead of the signal phrase.

quizzes.title: Vocabulary Quiz — Words of Crusade & Disguise

questions.text: The king moves among his people disguised as a tall palmer from the Holy Land. A palmer is —

answers.text: a pilgrim who has traveled to the Holy Land
a member of the king's guard

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a palmer is a pilgrim from the Holy Land, the perfect disguise for a wandering king.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A palmer is a religious traveler, not a weapon, an officer, or a guard.

questions.text: King Richard grants Robin a full pardon, canceling the outlaw charge. A pardon —

answers.text: officially forgives a crime and cancels its punishment
is a public contest of knights

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a pardon forgives a crime and cancels its punishment; Richard's pardon clears Robin's name.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A pardon is official forgiveness of a crime, not armor, a contest, or a traveler.

questions.text: The king's pardon brings a reconciliation between the rightful ruler and the outlaw band. Reconciliation means —

answers.text: the making of peace and the mending of a broken relationship

questions.feedback_correct: Right — reconciliation is making peace and restoring a broken relationship, just what happens between king and outlaw.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reconciliation is about mending a relationship, not a contest, an object, or an officer.

questions.text: A verderer, in the book, is —

answers.text: a pilgrim from the Holy Land
an officer who enforced the harsh royal Forest Laws

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a verderer enforced the Forest Laws; Robin shoots fifteen of them in his grief.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A verderer is a forest-law officer, not a cloth, a pilgrim, or a kingdom.

questions.text: Which sentence uses Crusade correctly?

answers.text: "He drew his Crusade and faced the knight."
"She wore a Crusade of white silk."
"King Richard left England to fight in the Crusade in the Holy Land."
"The Crusade pardoned Robin and his band."

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a Crusade was one of the medieval wars fought to control the Holy Land; Richard left to join it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A Crusade is a war, not a weapon, a cloth, or a person who can grant a pardon.

quizzes.title: Module 4 Outro — Robin Hood Wrap-Up
quizzes.description:
📋 Module wrap-up

This survey looks back over the eight weeks of Roger Lancelyn Green's The Adventures of Robin Hood and the module's essential question: What makes a true hero — and what happens when justice and law are not the same thing?

Full credit for honest, thoughtful responses. The survey helps the teacher understand how the module landed.

questions.text:
Revisit the module's essential question: "What makes a true hero — and what happens when justice and law are not the same thing?"

In 3–5 sentences, write the best answer to that question, one worth standing behind. Make a specific claim, name at least one piece of evidence from Green's text, and acknowledge the strongest version of the opposing view.
How confident are you that your final essay answered the essential question well?

answers.text: 4 — Very confident: I made a specific, arguable claim with strong evidence.
3 — Mostly confident: My claim is clear but I wish the evidence or explanation were stronger.
2 — Somewhat confident: I have an answer but I'm not sure how well I argued it.
1 — Not very confident: I'm still not sure what my claim really is.

questions.text: Name one specific thing from this module that changed how you read — not what you know, but how you read. For example: a grammar tool, a way of looking at evidence, a habit of asking "why does the author do this?" — something you now do automatically that you didn't do in Week 1.

What is still unclear to you? Name one specific question or idea from the module that you didn't fully get — or that you understand in a general way but couldn't explain precisely if someone asked. Be specific: "I didn't understand everything" is not useful; "I understand that the Sheriff is a symbol of systemic injustice but I'm not sure what that actually means" is.
Which of the seven virtues did this module ask the most of you personally?

answers.text: Courage — taking a position when I wasn't sure I was right.
Honesty — representing the text accurately even when it complicated my argument.
Perseverance — finishing the essay even when revision was hard.
Self-government — managing my time and attention across eight weeks.
Responsibility — turning in quality work because the work matters, not just for the grade.
Service — contributing to discussions in a way that helped my classmates think.
Courtesy — engaging seriously with views I disagreed with.

questions.text: Is there anything the module should have done differently, or anything the teacher should know about the experience of it? Topics can include pacing, the essay scaffolding, the texts, or the discussions. This is optional and purely for the teacher's information.

quizzes.title: Grammar Quiz — Revision & Sentence Variety

questions.text: What does revision mainly mean?

answers.text: Re-seeing and reshaping a draft so it argues better

questions.feedback_correct: Right — revision is re-seeing and reshaping your draft, not just fixing surface errors.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Revision reshapes the writing to argue better; fixing spelling alone is editing, not revising.

questions.text: Which is the best way to combine these choppy sentences? "Robin is an outlaw. Robin is also just."

answers.text: Robin is an outlaw. Robin is just.
Robin is an outlaw, but he is also just.
Robin is an outlaw, Robin is just.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — joining the two ideas with but keeps the flow and removes the repeated subject.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Combine the two ideas into one smooth sentence with a conjunction; option D is a comma splice.

questions.text: Which sentence shows the best varied opening (not starting with the subject)?

answers.text: Robin forbids revenge on the Prioress.
Dying in Marian's arms, Robin forbids revenge on the Prioress.
Robin is dying and Robin forbids revenge.
Robin. He forbids revenge on the Prioress.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — opening with a describing phrase varies the rhythm instead of starting with Robin again.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A varied opening begins with something other than the subject, such as a describing phrase or a time word.

questions.text: Why does varying your sentence openings help your essay?

answers.text: It keeps the writing from sounding repetitive and is easier to read

questions.feedback_correct: Right — when sentences stop starting the same way, the writing flows and holds the reader.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Varying openings improves flow and readability; it does not shorten the essay or add citations.

questions.text: Which revision best combines these into one sentence? "King Richard died. Then John became king. John hunted Robin."

answers.text: King Richard died. John became king. John hunted Robin.
King Richard died, John became king, John hunted Robin.
After King Richard died, John became king and hunted Robin.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a varied opening (After King Richard died) plus a conjunction joins three choppy sentences into one clear one.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Combine the three short sentences into one; option B is a comma splice and option A leaves them choppy.

quizzes.title: Vocabulary Quiz — Words of Sanctuary & Legacy

questions.text: Robin sends Marian to seek sanctuary with the Prioress. Sanctuary here means —

answers.text: safety or protection given in a holy place

questions.feedback_correct: Right — sanctuary is the protection a holy place such as a nunnery gives someone in danger.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Sanctuary is safety given in a holy place, not a betrayal, a person, or an ending.

questions.text: The Prioress of Kirkleys betrays Robin. A Prioress is —

answers.text: the nun who leads a priory or nunnery

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a Prioress leads a priory or nunnery; this one covets Robin's estate and kills him.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A Prioress is the nun who leads a nunnery, not a legacy, a pilgrim, or sanctuary itself.

questions.text: The Prioress's treachery ends Robin's life. Treachery means —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — treachery is a betrayal of trust; the Prioress pretends to help, then kills him.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Treachery is a betrayal of trust, not courage, a contest, or forgiveness.

questions.text: Long after his death, Robin's legacy lives on as a legend. A legacy is —

answers.text: a war in the Holy Land
what a person leaves behind after death

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a legacy is what a person leaves behind, such as a reputation, an example, or a story.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A legacy is what a person leaves behind, not an object, a war, or an officer.

questions.text: Which sentence uses mercy correctly?

answers.text: "He drew his mercy and fired an arrow."
"Even though she had killed him, Robin showed mercy and forbade revenge."
"Marian sought mercy with the Prioress for safety."
"The mercy enforced the harsh Forest Laws."

questions.feedback_correct: Right — mercy is kindness or forgiveness toward someone you could harm; Robin's refusal of revenge is mercy.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Mercy is forgiveness toward someone you could punish, not a weapon, a refuge, or an officer.

quizzes.title: Module 5 Intro — Before We Begin
quizzes.description:
📋 Before we begin

Answer the questions below before beginning Module 5: The Bronze Bow. This is a short reflection survey. There are no right or wrong answers, and responses are not graded for correctness; the teacher uses them to see where the class is starting.

Reading access & copyright. Students must obtain lawful access to the assigned literary work separately. Optima course materials are original instructional materials designed to support analysis, discussion, and assessment of the work. Copyrighted text, images, illustrations, panels, audio, or other protected materials are not reproduced in Canvas, videos, downloadable files, or teacher resources except where expressly licensed, in the public domain, or approved as a limited fair-use excerpt for instructional analysis.

Students read The Bronze Bow by Elizabeth George Speare from their own copy of the book.

questions.text:
Here is the essential question for this module:

"Can love accomplish what hatred cannot?"

Write 2–4 sentences giving your first, honest answer. This question returns at the end of the module. Do not research an answer; write the current thinking.

This module follows Daniel, a young man whose family was destroyed under Roman occupation and who has organized his life around hatred. How familiar are you with historical fiction — stories set in a real time and place from the past?

answers.text: Very familiar — I read and enjoy historical fiction often.
Somewhat familiar — I have read some.
Not very familiar — historical settings are new for me.

questions.text: The module project is an argumentative essay that takes a position and defends it. How confident do you feel right now about writing an argument that states a claim and backs it with evidence?

answers.text: Very confident — I have written arguments before.
Somewhat confident — I can do it but want practice.
A little nervous — arguing a position is hard for me.
Not confident — I am not sure how to build an argument.

questions.text: Name one thing you are curious about before starting this module — about the novel, about first-century Judea, or about the question of whether love can do what hatred cannot.
Have you read the checklist for this module (the weekly lessons, quizzes, Quick Writes, discussions, and the project essay)?

answers.text: Yes — I have read the checklist and know what is due each week.
Not yet — I will read it before starting Week 1.

quizzes.title: Grammar Quiz — Proper Nouns & Sentence Types

questions.text: Which word in this sentence is a proper noun? "Daniel walked to the busy town of Capernaum."
questions.feedback_correct: A proper noun names one specific place — Capernaum — and is always capitalized.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Town" names any town; "busy" describes; "walked" is an action. Which word names one specific place?

questions.text: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?

answers.text: Daniel lives in Galilee, near the Sea of Galilee.
daniel lives in galilee, near the sea of galilee.
Daniel lives in galilee, near the Sea of galilee.
Daniel Lives In Galilee, Near The Sea Of Galilee.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — names of people and places (Daniel, Galilee, Sea of Galilee) are capitalized; ordinary words are not.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Capitalize proper nouns (Daniel, Galilee), not every word and not none of them.

questions.text: What type of sentence is this? "Why does Daniel hate the Romans?"
questions.feedback_correct: Right — it asks a question and ends in a question mark, so it is interrogative.
questions.feedback_incorrect: This sentence asks something. A sentence that asks a question is interrogative.

questions.text: Which sentence is imperative (gives a command or request)?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — it tells someone to do something, so it is imperative.
questions.feedback_incorrect: An imperative sentence gives a command or request. Which choice tells someone to do something?

questions.text: Which sentence correctly matches its end mark to an exclamatory sentence (strong feeling)?

answers.text: Daniel met Joel on the mountain.
They have taken everything from us!

questions.feedback_correct: Right — strong feeling plus an exclamation point makes this exclamatory.
questions.feedback_incorrect: An exclamatory sentence shows strong feeling and ends with an exclamation point.

quizzes.title: Vocabulary Quiz — Words of Occupied Galilee

questions.text: A line of Roman legionaries marched along the road. Legionaries are —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — legionaries are Rome's foot soldiers, the men who enforce its rule.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Legionaries are soldiers, not prayer boxes, chains, or priests.

questions.text: On the Sabbath the people gathered in the synagogue. A synagogue is —

answers.text: a building where Jewish people gather to pray and hear the Scriptures

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a synagogue is where Jewish people gather to pray and hear the Scriptures read.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A synagogue is a place of prayer and reading, not a palace, a fort, or a shop.

questions.text: Daniel filed the heavy iron manacles off the freed slave's wrists. Manacles are —

answers.text: iron rings and chains locked on the wrists

questions.feedback_correct: Right — manacles are the iron rings and chains used to hold a prisoner or slave.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Manacles are restraints locked on the wrists, not coins, cloaks, or jars.

questions.text: Joel called the blacksmith "Simon the Zealot." A Zealot was —

answers.text: a member of the movement that wanted to drive Rome out by force

questions.feedback_correct: Right — Zealots wanted to free Israel from Rome by force.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A Zealot fought Roman rule; the word does not mean a tax collector, merchant, or beggar.

questions.text: Which sentence uses the word vow correctly?

answers.text: "He sharpened his vow on the stone before the battle."
"She wore a vow of fine silk to the feast."
"Daniel made a vow to fight Rome with his whole life."
"The vow galloped down the road on a fast horse."

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a vow is a solemn promise; Daniel vows to fight Rome.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A vow is a serious promise, not a thing you sharpen, wear, or ride.

quizzes.title: Grammar Quiz — Verb Tenses

questions.text: What tense is the verb in this sentence? "Daniel spared the old miser."
questions.feedback_correct: Right — spared shows an action that already happened, so it is past tense.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The action is already over. A verb showing a finished action is in the past tense.

questions.text: What tense is the verb phrase? "Daniel will lead the band of boys."
questions.feedback_correct: Right — will lead uses the helping word will for an action that has not happened yet, so it is future.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The word will is a clue. An action that has not happened yet is in the future tense.

questions.text: What tense is the verb? "Daniel works at the smithy every day."
questions.feedback_correct: Right — works shows an action happening now or generally true, so it is present tense.
questions.feedback_incorrect: This action happens now, day after day. A verb for what is happening now is present tense.

questions.text: Which sentence has no tense shift (the verbs stay in one tense)?

answers.text: Daniel cares for Leah and worked all day.
Daniel cared for Leah and works all day.
Daniel cares for Leah and will worked all day.
Daniel cared for Leah and worked all day.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — both verbs (cared, worked) are past tense, so there is no shift.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the choice where both verbs are in the same tense. Mixing past and present is a tense shift.

questions.text: This sentence shifts tense by mistake: "Daniel walks to the village and spared the miser." What is the best fix?

answers.text: Daniel walk to the village and spare the miser.
Daniel walked to the village and spared the miser.
Daniel walks to the village and will spared the miser.
Daniel walking to the village and spared the miser.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — putting both verbs in the past (walked, spared) keeps the tense steady.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Choose the fix that puts both verbs in the same tense. "Walked" and "spared" are both past.

quizzes.title: Vocabulary Quiz — Words of the Village

questions.text: Rosh sent Daniel to rob a greedy old miser. A miser is —

answers.text: a person who hoards money and hates to spend it

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a miser hoards money and will not spend it; Daniel is sent to rob one.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A miser is about hoarding money, not a soldier, a story, or a tool.

questions.text: Jesus taught the crowd with a parable. A parable is —

answers.text: a short, simple story that teaches a deeper truth

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a parable is a short story that teaches a lesson or deeper truth.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A parable is a teaching story, not a tax, a sword, or a gift.

questions.text: At the forge, Daniel struck the hot iron against the anvil. An anvil is —

answers.text: a heavy iron block a blacksmith hammers metal against

questions.feedback_correct: Right — an anvil is the heavy iron block a smith hammers metal on.
questions.feedback_incorrect: An anvil is a blacksmith's iron block, not a pouch, cloth, or story.

questions.text: Leah's coins would one day be her dowry. A dowry is —

answers.text: money or goods a bride brings to a marriage

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a dowry is the money or goods a bride brings to a marriage.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A dowry has to do with marriage, not a punishment, a bird, or a law.

questions.text: Which sentence uses the word conscience correctly?

answers.text: "He hammered the conscience flat on the anvil."
"She wove a conscience of fine wool at the loom."
"The conscience galloped down the road on a horse."
"After the robbery, Daniel's conscience would not let him rest."

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a conscience is the inner sense of right and wrong; Daniel's troubles him.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A conscience is an inner sense of right and wrong, not an object you hammer, weave, or ride.

quizzes.title: Grammar Quiz — Adjectives & Appositives

questions.text: Which word in this sentence is an adjective? "The silent giant tore the chains apart."
questions.feedback_correct: An adjective describes a noun — silent tells what kind of giant.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Giant" and "chains" name things; "tore" is an action. Which word describes the giant?

questions.text: An appositive is —

answers.text: a word that shows an action
a noun phrase placed beside another noun to rename it
a word that joins two sentences
a word that shows when something happens

questions.feedback_correct: Right — an appositive renames the noun beside it, as in "Samson, the giant, …"
questions.feedback_incorrect: Actions are verbs; joining words are conjunctions. An appositive renames a nearby noun.

questions.text: In "Marcus, a German soldier, kept watch over the house," the appositive is —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — "a German soldier" renames Marcus and sits right beside his name, set off by commas.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The appositive renames Marcus. Which phrase tells us who Marcus is?

questions.text: Which sentence punctuates the appositive correctly?

answers.text: Daniel the band's new leader planned the rescue.
Daniel, the band's new leader, planned the rescue.
Daniel, the band's new leader planned the rescue.
Daniel the band's new leader, planned the rescue.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — an appositive that adds extra information takes a comma on each side.
questions.feedback_incorrect: An appositive that adds extra information needs a comma before and after it.

questions.text: Which sentence uses an appositive to rename a character?

answers.text: The giant was strong and silent.
Daniel ran quickly to warn Jesus.
Joel, the scribe's son, was sent to the galleys.
Rosh refused to help with the rescue.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — "the scribe's son" renames Joel, set off with commas. That is an appositive.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for a noun phrase that renames a character, set off by commas. Which sentence does that?

quizzes.title: Vocabulary Quiz — Words of the Turning

questions.text: The Romans warned of a harsh reprisal against any village that sheltered the rescuers. Reprisal means —

answers.text: punishment given in return for a wrong

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a reprisal is punishment delivered as payback for an attack or wrong.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A reprisal is about payback by force, not a holiday, a weapon, or a unit of men.

questions.text: Marcus tells Leah his cohort is being transferred to a far city. A cohort is —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — a cohort is a unit of Roman soldiers, part of a legion.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A cohort is a group of soldiers, not a holiday, a machine, or a delegation.

questions.text: On the Day of Atonement the people fasted and prayed. Atonement means —

answers.text: making up for a wrong; setting things right

questions.feedback_correct: Right — atonement is making up for a wrong and setting it right; the Day of Atonement is a holy day of repair.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Atonement is about repairing a wrong, not a tax, a weapon, or a place.

questions.text: As Jesus passed, the crowd cried out that the Messiah had come at last. A Messiah is —

answers.text: the promised deliverer the people hoped for

questions.feedback_correct: Right — the Messiah is the long-awaited deliverer; the crowd hoped Jesus was the one.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The Messiah is the awaited deliverer, not an officer, a machine, or a festival.

questions.text: Which sentence uses vengeance correctly?

answers.text: "The vengeance was a heavy iron block in the smith's shop."
"For years Daniel had lived for vengeance against the Romans."
"She wore a vengeance of fine cloth to the festival."
"The soldiers marched in a vengeance through the town."

questions.feedback_correct: Right — vengeance is harm done to pay back a wrong; Daniel lived for revenge against Rome.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Vengeance is revenge, not an object, a garment, or a group of soldiers.

quizzes.title: Grammar Quiz — Commas & Participial Phrases

questions.text: In "Crossing the road, Daniel asked Marcus inside," the participial phrase is —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — "Crossing the road" is built on an -ing verb and describes Daniel. That is a participial phrase.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A participial phrase is built on an -ing or -ed verb and describes a noun. Which phrase describes Daniel?

questions.text: A participle is —

answers.text: a word that joins two sentences
a word that names a person or thing
a verb form (often -ing or -ed) used to describe a noun
a word that shows when something happens

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a participle (trembling, healed) is a verb form that describes a noun.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Joining words are conjunctions; naming words are nouns. A participle describes a noun.

questions.text: Which sentence places the comma correctly after the opening phrase?

answers.text: Healed by Jesus Leah smiled at last.
Healed, by Jesus Leah smiled at last.
Healed by Jesus, Leah smiled at last.
Healed by Jesus Leah, smiled at last.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — an opening participial phrase takes a comma right after it, before the noun it describes.
questions.feedback_incorrect: When a participial phrase opens a sentence, the comma goes after the whole phrase, before the noun.

questions.text: Which sentence aims the participial phrase at the right noun (no dangling phrase)?

answers.text: Healed by Jesus, Leah felt the fever leave her.
Healed by Jesus, the room felt lighter to everyone.
Healed by Jesus, the goat had already died.
Healed by Jesus, the road seemed shorter.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — Leah is the one healed, so the phrase describes the correct noun.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The phrase must describe the noun right after the comma. Who can actually be "healed by Jesus"?

questions.text: Which sentence uses an opening participial phrase correctly?

answers.text: Daniel asked Marcus inside crossing the road.
Trembling with fear, Leah reached for her brother's hand.
Marcus kept watch and the road.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — "Trembling with fear" opens the sentence, takes a comma, and describes Leah.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for an -ing or -ed phrase that opens the sentence, is set off by a comma, and describes the next noun.

quizzes.title: Vocabulary Quiz — Words of Healing and Home

questions.text: The physician looked down at the feverish Leah and shook his head. A physician is —

answers.text: a doctor who treats the sick

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a physician is a doctor; he despairs of helping Leah before Jesus comes.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A physician treats the sick. He is not a soldier, an object, or a promise.

questions.text: Daniel warned Marcus never to cross the threshold of his house. A threshold is —

answers.text: the doorway or entrance of a house

questions.feedback_correct: Right — the threshold is the doorway; Daniel forbids it, then opens it to Marcus.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A threshold is a doorway, not a machine, a holiday, or a group of men.

questions.text: Marcus kept a vigil across the road, watching and waiting for word of Leah. A vigil is —

answers.text: a period of staying awake to watch over someone

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a vigil is a watchful waiting; Marcus stays awake across the road, hoping to say goodbye.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A vigil is a watchful waiting, not a cloth, a tax, or a weapon.

questions.text: The text says Leah was betrayed by the one thing she still reached out to. Betrayed means —

answers.text: let down or harmed by something trusted

questions.feedback_correct: Right — to be betrayed is to be let down by someone or something you trusted.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Betrayed means harmed by something trusted, not healed, praised, or paid.

questions.text: Which sentence uses mezuzah correctly?

answers.text: "The soldiers fired the mezuzah at the city wall."
"He touched the mezuzah on the doorpost as he passed into the house."
"She wore a mezuzah of white silk to the feast."
"The mezuzah marched through the village at dawn."

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a mezuzah is a small case of Scripture on a doorpost, touched as one passes through the door.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A mezuzah is a small case on a doorpost, not a weapon, a garment, or a group of soldiers.

quizzes.title: Module 5 Outro — Looking Back
quizzes.description:
📋 Looking back

Reflect on Module 5: The Bronze Bow: the novel, Daniel's change from hatred to love, and the written argument. Responses are not graded for correctness and help the teacher plan follow-up support.

questions.text:
Return to the essential question:

"Can love accomplish what hatred cannot?"

Write 3–5 sentences giving your answer now, at the end of the module. Look back at what you wrote in the intro survey. Has your answer changed? What in the novel — or in your own essay — moved you?
How confident do you feel now about writing an argument that states a claim, fairly considers the other side, and defends it with evidence?

What is still unclear to you, or what would you most like more practice with — building an argument that answers the other side fairly, using evidence, the three ways writers persuade (logos, ethos, pathos), or a grammar tool from this module?

This module asked something of readers and writers. Which of the seven virtues did The Bronze Bow most ask you to think about? Choose one, then write 2–3 sentences explaining your choice — using Daniel, or your own work, as evidence.

  • Courage
  • Courtesy
  • Honesty
  • Perseverance
  • Self-government
  • Service
  • Responsibility
How ready do you feel to start the next module?

answers.text: Ready — I feel good about what I learned here.
Mostly ready — a few things I want to review first.
I would like to check in with my teacher before moving on.

quizzes.title: Grammar Quiz — Parallel Structure, Colons & Semicolons

questions.text: Which sentence has correct parallel structure?

answers.text: Daniel vowed to hate them, fighting them, and that he would kill them.
Daniel vowed hating them, to fight, and killing.
Daniel vowed to hate them, to fight them, and to kill them.
Daniel vowed to hate, fights, and killing them.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — every part is "to" plus a verb (to hate, to fight, to kill), so the list is parallel.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Parallel structure keeps each listed part in the same form. Which choice repeats "to" plus a verb all the way through?

questions.text: A colon is used correctly in —

answers.text: Daniel faced: Rosh, Hezron, and Jesus.
Daniel faced three voices: Rosh, Hezron, and Jesus.
Three voices were: that Daniel had to choose among.
Daniel: faced three voices that pulled at him.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a full sentence ("Daniel faced three voices") comes before the colon, and the colon introduces the list.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A colon needs a complete sentence before it, then introduces a list or explanation. Which choice does that?

questions.text: A semicolon is used correctly in —

answers.text: Rosh chose the sword; Jesus chose love.
Rosh chose the sword; and Jesus, love.
Rosh chose; the sword while Jesus chose love.
Rosh chose the sword; because he hated Rome.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a semicolon joins two complete, related sentences. "Rosh chose the sword" and "Jesus chose love" can each stand alone.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A semicolon links two complete sentences. Which choice has a full sentence on both sides, with no joining word like "and" or "because"?

questions.text: Which list is parallel?

answers.text: Carrying Leah, to spare the miser, the rescue
He carried Leah, spares the miser, leading the rescue
Carry Leah, sparing the miser, led the rescue
Carrying Leah, sparing the miser, leading the rescue

questions.feedback_correct: Right — every item uses the -ing form (carrying, sparing, leading), so the list is parallel.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A parallel list keeps every item in the same form. Which choice keeps every item in the -ing form?

questions.text: Which mark best fills the blank? "Daniel made a choice no sword could make ___ he chose to love his enemy."
questions.feedback_correct: Right — a full sentence comes first, and the colon introduces the explanation of the choice.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The first part is a complete sentence, and what follows explains it. Which single mark introduces an explanation?

quizzes.title: Vocabulary Quiz — Words of the Argument

questions.text: Your essay's thesis is —

answers.text: a list of every event in the book
the one debatable claim you set out to prove

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a thesis is the single debatable claim your whole essay argues for.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A thesis is not a summary or a list. It is the one claim you prove.

questions.text: Daniel's vow to harm the Romans for killing his father is an act of vengeance. Vengeance means —

answers.text: harm done in return for a wrong; revenge

questions.feedback_correct: Right — vengeance is harm done in return for a wrong. Daniel's vow is built on it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Vengeance is about getting back at someone for a wrong, not a promise, a belief, or making peace.

questions.text: By the last chapter, Daniel has undergone a complete transformation. Transformation means —

answers.text: a complete change in someone or something

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a transformation is a complete change. Daniel's runs from hatred to love.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Transformation is about a deep change in a person, not an object, a tax, or a feast.

questions.text: After stating your thesis, you fairly state the counterargument. A counterargument is —

answers.text: a second copy of your thesis
the strongest case against your claim, which you then answer
the last sentence of your essay

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a counterargument is the best objection to your claim; you state it fairly, then answer it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A counterargument is the other side's best case, not a quotation, a repeat of your thesis, or a closing line.

questions.text: Which sentence uses reconcile correctly?

answers.text: "He reconciled his sword before the battle."
"The reconcile rose over the Sea of Galilee."
"She wore a reconcile of white cloth."
"In the end, Daniel reconciles with the enemy he once hated, inviting Marcus into his home."

questions.feedback_correct: Right — to reconcile is to make peace after conflict. Daniel reconciles with Marcus at the end.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reconcile is a verb meaning to make peace, not a weapon, an object, or a thing in the sky.

quizzes.title: Module 6 Intro — Before We Begin
quizzes.description:
📋 Before we begin

Module 6: Shakespeare Stories is the last module of the year. The questions below have no right or wrong answers; the teacher uses the responses to see where the class is starting. The survey is not graded for correctness.

Reading access & copyright. The Shakespeare tales for this module — Charles and Mary Lamb's Tales from Shakespeare — are in the public domain and are provided right in the lessons, so nothing needs to be bought to read them. If your capstone reaches back to an earlier-year novel (St. George and the Dragon, King Arthur, Robin Hood, The Bronze Bow), use your own copy of that book.

Students must obtain lawful access to any assigned copyrighted literary work separately. Optima course materials are original instructional materials designed to support analysis, discussion, and assessment of the work. Copyrighted text, images, illustrations, panels, audio, or other protected materials are not reproduced in Canvas, videos, downloadable files, or teacher resources except where expressly licensed, in the public domain, or approved as a limited fair-use excerpt for instructional analysis.

questions.text:
Here is the essential question for this module:

"Of everything you have read this year, what lasts — and what makes it worth carrying forward?"

Write 2–4 sentences giving your first, honest answer. The question returns at the end of the module. Write the current thinking without researching.
Before this module begins, how much do you already know about Shakespeare?

answers.text: I know a lot — I have read Shakespeare or seen his plays performed
I know a little — I have heard of the famous plays and characters
I know almost nothing — the name is familiar but that is about it
I have never heard of Shakespeare before

questions.text: Which of these four year-end themes do you think is most important for a person to have?

answers.text: Heroism — the courage to do the right thing at great personal cost
Self-Sacrifice — the willingness to give up something precious for others
Happiness — the wisdom to know what actually makes a life worth living
Duty — the commitment to answer a call even when it is hard

questions.text: How do you feel about reading plays and dramatic stories (as opposed to novels or short stories)?

answers.text: I love plays — I enjoy how characters reveal themselves through dialogue
Plays are fine — a different experience, but I can work with them
I find plays harder to follow than novels
I have never read a play before, so I am not sure

questions.text: Think back over all the books and stories you have read this year. Which character has stayed with you the most, and why? (You do not have to be sure — this is your starting point for the Module Project.)

This module's final project includes an optional group-work track for one part of the planning. Would you like to opt in? (The teacher will follow up with details if the answer is yes. Choosing no does not affect your grade in any way.)

answers.text: Yes, I am interested in the group-work option.
No, I prefer to complete the project independently.
I am not sure yet — I would like to learn more before deciding.

quizzes.title: Grammar Quiz — Appositives

questions.text: An appositive is —

answers.text: a word that shows an action
a noun phrase placed beside another noun to rename or explain it
a word that joins two sentences
a word that describes a verb

questions.feedback_correct: Right — an appositive renames the noun next to it, usually set off by commas.
questions.feedback_incorrect: An appositive renames a noun (like "Prospero, the duke of Milan"), not an action or a joining word.

questions.text: In "Ariel, a faithful spirit, served Prospero," which words are the appositive?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — "a faithful spirit" renames Ariel and sits between commas, so it is the appositive.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The appositive renames Ariel. Which words could you lift out and still have a sentence?

questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses an appositive with commas to combine "Miranda was a princess" and "Miranda had never seen another man"?

answers.text: Miranda, a princess, had never seen another man.
