Miranda a princess had never seen another man.
Miranda was a princess had never seen another man.
Miranda had never seen another man a princess.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — the appositive "a princess" sits between two commas and renames Miranda.
questions.feedback_incorrect: An appositive needs a comma before and after it, and it should sit right beside the noun it renames.

questions.text: In "Antonio, Prospero's false brother, seized the dukedom," the appositive renames which noun?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — "Prospero's false brother" renames Antonio, telling us who he is.
questions.feedback_incorrect: An appositive renames the noun right before it. Who is "Prospero's false brother"?

questions.text: Which sentence punctuates its appositive correctly?

answers.text: Gonzalo the kind old lord, saved the books.
Gonzalo, the kind old lord saved the books.
Gonzalo the kind old lord saved the books.
Gonzalo, the kind old lord, saved the books.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — an appositive in the middle of a sentence needs a comma before and after it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The appositive "the kind old lord" needs a comma on both sides, not just one or none.

quizzes.title: Vocabulary Quiz — Words from The Tempest

questions.text: The witch Sycorax had enchanted the whole island. Enchanted means —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — to enchant something is to place it under a magic spell.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Enchanted is about magic, not fire, kings, or water. Sycorax used her magic on the island.

questions.text: Ariel was sure the prisoners' penitence was sincere. Penitence means —

answers.text: real sorrow for having done wrong

questions.feedback_correct: Right — penitence is real sorrow for a wrong you have done; the king and Antonio were truly sorry.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Penitence is about being genuinely sorry, not wealth, travel, or trickery.

questions.text: Prospero set Ferdinand hard tasks only to test his constancy in love. Constancy means —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — constancy is staying faithful and steady; Prospero wanted to be sure Ferdinand's love would not change.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Constancy is about being steady and faithful, not strength, anger, or sadness.

questions.text: The lively little sprite Ariel obeyed Prospero. A sprite is —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — a sprite is a small, lively spirit; Lamb calls Ariel exactly that.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A sprite is a spirit, not an object, a ship, or a book. Ariel is the "lively little sprite."

questions.text: Which sentence uses reconciliation correctly?

answers.text: "He sharpened his reconciliation before the battle."
"The reconciliation rose from the sea holding a sword."
"She wore a reconciliation of white silk."
"After Prospero forgave his brother, their reconciliation made old Gonzalo weep for joy."

questions.feedback_correct: Right — reconciliation is becoming friendly again after a quarrel, exactly what happens at the tale's end.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reconciliation is the act of making peace after a quarrel, not a weapon, a person, or a cloth.

quizzes.title: Grammar Quiz — Punctuating Dialogue

questions.text: Which line of dialogue is punctuated correctly?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — quotation marks wrap the spoken words, a comma joins them to the tag, and the comma sits inside the quotes.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The comma goes inside the closing quotation mark, just before the speaker tag "said Beatrice."

questions.text: When the speaker tag comes first, which line is correct?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — put a comma after the tag, then capitalize the first word of the quoted sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Tag first needs a comma after it, and the quoted sentence still begins with a capital letter.

questions.text: Where does the question mark go in a spoken question?

answers.text: it is replaced by a comma

questions.feedback_correct: Right — the question mark belongs to the spoken words, so it goes inside the closing quotation mark: "How does the lady?" he asked.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The question mark belongs to what the character said, so it stays inside the quotation marks.

questions.text: In writing a back-and-forth conversation, you should start a new paragraph —

answers.text: only at the start of the page
never; keep it all in one paragraph

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a new paragraph for each new speaker lets the reader follow who is talking.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The rule is "new speaker, new paragraph," so the reader never loses track of who is speaking.

questions.text: Which line places all the punctuation correctly?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — the question mark sits inside the closing quote, and the tag follows in lowercase.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The spoken words and their question mark belong inside the quotation marks; the tag "he asked" comes after.

quizzes.title: Vocabulary Quiz — Words from Much Ado About Nothing

questions.text: Beatrice and Benedick kept up a war of raillery. Raillery means —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — raillery is good-humored teasing; the two wits trade it whenever they meet.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Raillery is about playful teasing, not armor, a feast, or an oath.

questions.text: The friar hoped to turn the slander against Hero into pity. Slander means —

answers.text: false words spoken to harm a good name

questions.feedback_correct: Right — slander is false speech meant to damage someone's reputation, exactly what is done to Hero.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Slander is false, harmful speech about a person, not a shelter, a faint, or a joke.

questions.text: Shocked by the accusation, Hero fell down in a swoon. A swoon is —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — a swoon is a faint; Hero collapses from the shock of being falsely accused.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A swoon is a faint, not a promise, a remark, or a plot.

questions.text: Claudio promised to do whatever penance Leonato asked. Penance means —

answers.text: an act done to make up for a wrong

questions.feedback_correct: Right — penance is an act done to make up for a wrong; Claudio accepts it for falsely accusing Hero.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Penance is about making up for a wrong you have done, not a game, a voyage, or clothing.

questions.text: Which sentence uses arbour correctly?

answers.text: "She drew her arbour and pointed it at the enemy."
"He swallowed the bitter arbour the doctor gave him."
"The prince crowned the new arbour of Messina."
"Benedick sat reading in the shady arbour among the trees."

questions.feedback_correct: Right — an arbour is a shady garden shelter made of trees or vines; Benedick reads in one.
questions.feedback_incorrect: An arbour is a leafy garden shelter, not a weapon, a medicine, or a title.

quizzes.title: Module 6 Outro — Looking Back on the Year
quizzes.description:
📋 Looking back on the year

This reflection follows Module 6: Shakespeare Stories and the year of reading. Complete it before submitting the final project. The teacher reads every response. There are no right or wrong answers.

questions.text:
Here again is the module's essential question:

"Of everything you have read this year, what lasts — and what makes it worth carrying forward?"

Write 3–5 sentences giving your answer now — after reading the Shakespeare tales, completing the year-in-review, and building your Module Project. How has your answer changed since the start of the module? What changed it?
How confident do you feel writing a paragraph or essay that argues a claim and supports it with specific evidence from a text?

answers.text: 5 — Very confident. I know how to do this.
4 — Mostly confident. I can do it with some effort.
3 — Somewhat confident. I am still working on it.
2 — Not very confident. This is still hard for me.
1 — Not confident at all. I feel lost when I try.

questions.text: What is one thing from this module or this year that still feels unclear or unfinished to you — a question the reading raised that you have not resolved, a writing skill that did not fully click, or an idea you want to understand better?
Which of the seven Optima virtues did this module most require of you as a student?

answers.text: Courage — I had to take a position and defend it, even when it was uncomfortable.
Perseverance — I had to push through when the reading or the writing was hard.
Self-government — I had to manage my time and discipline my work across three weeks.
Honesty — I had to be truthful in my writing and represent the texts fairly.
Courtesy — I had to engage with other students' ideas with respect.
Responsibility — I had to complete all my work, including all my assignments and the capstone.
Service — I was thinking about what I was contributing to the class conversation.

questions.text: Which text from this entire year of reading was most meaningful to you?
Name one character from this year's reading that you think about differently now than when you first met them. Say what changed and why.
If you could recommend one book from this year to a friend who does not usually like reading, which would you choose, and what would you say about it?

quizzes.title: Grammar Quiz — Transitions & the Periodic Sentence

questions.text: A transition is a word or phrase that —

answers.text: names a person, place, or thing
shows the reader how two ideas connect

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a transition (likewise, in contrast, therefore) signals the relationship between two ideas.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Naming is a noun's job and replacing is a pronoun's. A transition shows how ideas connect.

questions.text: Two ideas are alike. Which transition signals that likeness?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — likewise tells the reader the next idea is similar to the one before it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "However," "in contrast," and "unlike" all signal a difference. Which word signals a likeness?

questions.text: "St. George reaches the people in time. ______, Midas learns his lesson only after the harm is done." Which transition best fits the difference between these ideas?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — the two ideas point in opposite directions, so a difference word like in contrast fits.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The two ideas are opposites (in time versus too late). "Similarly," "likewise," and "in the same way" all signal likeness.

questions.text: A periodic sentence is one that —

answers.text: holds its main point until the end

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a periodic sentence builds up first and lands its main point on the final words, which makes a strong closing.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Length and transitions are not what defines it. A periodic sentence saves its main point for the end.

questions.text: Which sentence is periodic (main point at the end)?

answers.text: "Across three stories, from three centuries, by three authors, the same truth keeps returning."
"The same truth returns in three stories from three centuries."
"Three stories return, and the truth is the same."
"The truth keeps returning, story after story, year after year, again and again."

questions.feedback_correct: Right — the buildup comes first and the main point ("the same truth keeps returning") lands at the very end.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The others state the main point early or trail off after it. Which one makes you wait until the final words for the point?

quizzes.title: Vocabulary Quiz — Words for Comparison & Argument

questions.text: A claim is —

answers.text: a list of events from a story
a statement you argue for, one a reader could reasonably dispute
a word that has no meaning

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a claim is the arguable point you set out to prove; your evidence supports it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A claim is not a list or a title. It is the arguable statement at the center of your essay.

questions.text: To contrast two characters is to —

answers.text: put them in the same chapter

questions.feedback_correct: Right — contrast shows differences; compare shows likenesses.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Showing likeness is compare. To contrast is to show how two things differ.

questions.text: In an essay, your evidence is —

answers.text: the specific moment from a text that supports your claim
the number of pages you read

questions.feedback_correct: Right — evidence is the exact moment in the book that proves your point, not a general trait.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Evidence is not an opinion or a title. It is the specific moment from the text that backs up your claim.

questions.text: Synthesis means —

answers.text: putting separate pieces together into one larger idea

questions.feedback_correct: Right — synthesis combines your three moments into a single statement of what they share.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Synthesis is not repetition or a list. It is combining separate pieces into one larger idea.

questions.text: "Courage is an ______ idea, returning in story after story across the centuries." Which word fits?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — enduring means lasting a long time, which fits an idea that keeps returning.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Sudden," "brief," and "hidden" all suggest the opposite of lasting. Which word means it continues through the years?

discussions.title: All-Class Forum 1 — Robin's Code
discussions.html:
PURPOSE: Take and defend a position on whether Robin's handling of the abbot's money is justice or theft, using a specific moment from Chapters 1 to 8.

Steps

  1. Answer this question: When Robin takes the abbot's money and hands it to Sir Richard, is that justice, or is it theft with a good reason attached? Arguing that the question is wrong is allowed, but the post must then say what the act is.
  2. State the position in the first sentence of the initial post.
  3. Name a specific scene, line, or description from Chapters 1 to 8 (for example, "in Chapter 7, when ___").
  4. Answer the strongest objection to the position. For a justice position, the strongest objection is that the abbot's money was legally his.
  5. Post first. Other posts stay hidden until the initial post is submitted.
  6. Reply to at least two classmates. Each reply adds a second piece of evidence, challenges a part of the reasoning and says why, or asks a question the writer could actually answer.

Requirements

  • Complete sentences; no text-speak or all-lowercase posts.
  • An initial post that answers every part of the prompt.
  • Replies that add, challenge, or ask. "I agree" and "good point" are not replies.
  • Posts that stay on the question. Other questions about the book go in the optional Questions about the book thread, which is ungraded and never penalized.
  • Original contributions: build on an existing post with something new, or take a different position.
  • Disagreement with the idea, not the person, kept courteous.

Submit

  • One initial post plus replies to at least two classmates in the Canvas discussion, before the week closes.

Done when

  • My first post takes a position in its first sentence.
  • I named a specific moment from Chapters 1 to 8.
  • I answered the strongest objection to my own position.
  • I replied to two classmates, and each reply adds, challenges, or asks.

discussions.title: All-Class Forum 2 — The Case for a Hero
discussions.html:
PURPOSE: Test the essay thesis in public by defending one moment from Chapters 1 to 17 against the strongest opposing argument before drafting.

Steps

  1. Name the moment in the first sentence of the post: the chapter and what happens. Choose one moment, not three and not a summary of the character.
  2. Explain what the moment proves about Robin, which quality it shows, and what would change the view.
  3. Answer the best objection to the chosen moment (the men Robin killed, his enjoyment of the fight, or his choice of which laws to break, for example) honestly.
  4. Reply to at least two classmates: one reply to a moment not yet considered, saying what it revealed, and one reply that tests a classmate's reasoning with an objection left unanswered.

Requirements

  • The question: What makes a true hero, and what happens when justice and law are not the same thing?
  • Write in complete sentences; the first post answers every part of the prompt and names a specific scene, line, or description (for example "in Chapter 7, when ___").
  • A reply adds, challenges, or asks; "I agree" and "good point" are not replies.
  • Stay on the question, and build on or differ from points already posted rather than restating them.
  • Disagree with the idea, not the person, and keep it courteous.
  • Optional: post a genuine question about the text to the Questions about the book thread at any time; it is ungraded and never penalized.

Submit

  • Native Canvas Discussion: one initial post plus replies to at least two classmates; replies unlock after the initial post.

Done when

  • The first post names one specific moment from Chapters 1 to 17 in its first sentence.
  • The post says what the moment proves and what would change the view.
  • The best objection to the moment is answered, not the easiest one.
  • Two classmates received replies, and one reply tests the reasoning.

discussions.title: All-Class Forum 1 — Two Kinds of Freedom
discussions.html:
PURPOSE: Argue which idea of freedom The Bronze Bow takes more seriously by the end of Chapter 23: freedom won by force, taken back from Rome, or the freedom Jesus describes, which is not about Rome at all.

Steps

  1. Answer the question: By the end of Chapter 23, which of the two does the book itself take more seriously, and how can you tell? The question asks what Speare has built the book to make a reader feel, not which freedom the writer prefers or which one Daniel has picked. Authors argue through what they choose to show, who they let be right, and what they make a reader watch happen.
  2. Write an initial post that takes a position in its first sentence.
  3. Name the moment: a specific scene, line, or description from Chapters 1–23, for example "in Chapter 19, when ___."
  4. Answer the strongest objection to the position. If the position is that the book favours the teacher on the hill, the strongest objection is that Daniel's anger is drawn so sympathetically. If the position is the opposite, it is what happens to the people who follow Rosh.
  5. Reply to at least two classmates. In each reply, add evidence for their claim that they did not use, challenge a part of their reasoning and say why, or ask something their post left open.

Requirements

  • Complete sentences; no text-speak and no all-lowercase posts.
  • The first post answers every part of the prompt and names a specific moment in the text (a scene, a line, a description), not "the book shows" but "in Chapter 7, when ___."
  • Each reply adds something, challenges something, or asks something. "I agree" and "good point" are not replies.
  • Stay on the question. Other questions about the book go in the optional Questions about the book thread (ungraded, never penalised); a genuine question there counts as an extra contribution.
  • Read existing posts first. Build on a point with something new, or take a different position; do not restate.
  • Disagree with the idea, not the person; keep replies courteous. Changing one's mind in public is acceptable.

Submit

  • Post in the Canvas discussion by the end of Week 3. Replies are visible only after the initial post is submitted.

Done when

  • The first post takes a position in its first sentence.
  • A specific moment from Chapters 1–23 is named.
  • The strongest objection to the position is answered.
  • Two classmates received replies, and each reply adds, challenges, or asks.

discussions.title: All-Class Forum 2 — Testing Your Argument
discussions.html:
PURPOSE: Test the claim the module essay will argue (can love accomplish what hatred cannot?) by posting it for the class to challenge.

Steps

  1. Write the initial post, answering all four parts below.
  2. Claim, in one sentence. The actual sentence to be argued, not a description of it.
  3. Strongest evidence. One moment from the novel, named by chapter, with what it shows and why it is the strongest evidence rather than something that merely fits.
  4. Appeal. Name whether the evidence works through logos (the logic of what follows from what), ethos (the credibility of who is speaking or acting), or pathos (what the reader is made to feel), and how that can be told. If more than one applies, say which carries the weight.
  5. Objection. The one not yet answered, not the easiest one.
  6. Reply to at least two classmates, testing something in each: the claim (give the counterexample from the novel it cannot handle), the appeal (say why the evidence works through a different one than named), or an unanswered objection (help answer it).

Requirements

  • Complete sentences; no text-speak and no all-lowercase posts.
  • The first post answers every part of the prompt and names a specific moment in the text (a scene, a line, a description), not "the book shows" but "in Chapter 7, when ___."
  • Each reply adds something, challenges something, or asks something. "I agree" and "good point" are not replies.
  • Stay on the question. Other questions about the book go in the optional Questions about the book thread (ungraded, never penalised); a genuine question there counts as an extra contribution.
  • Read existing posts first. Build on a point with something new, or take a different position; do not restate.
  • Disagree with the idea, not the person; keep replies courteous. Changing one's mind in public is acceptable.

Submit

  • Post in the Canvas discussion by the end of Week 5. Replies are visible only after the initial post is submitted.

Done when

  • The claim is one sentence and is the sentence planned for the essay.
  • One moment is named by chapter, with a reason it is the strongest evidence.
  • The appeal is named with a reason.
  • The objection named is a real one.
  • Two classmates received replies, and each reply tests something.

discussions.title: All-Class Forum 1 — Did Claudio Earn It?
discussions.html:
PURPOSE: Argue whether Claudio has earned the happy ending Shakespeare gives him in Much Ado About Nothing.

Steps

  1. Write a first post that answers all of the parts below. Replies stay hidden until the first post is submitted.
  2. Take a position in the first sentence: yes, no, or "partly, and here is the part."
  3. Name a specific moment, such as "when he says ___ at the wedding," not "he was mean to Hero."
  4. Answer the strongest objection to the position. If Claudio earned it, the strongest objection is that he never apologises to Hero herself. If he did not, it is that he was deceived by someone working hard to deceive him.
  5. Use at least one Module 6 vocabulary word correctly: usurper, enchantment, reconciliation, wit, slander, or repentance.
  6. Reply to at least two classmates by adding evidence, challenging their reasoning, or asking a question they could answer. At least one reply goes to a classmate who landed somewhere different.

Requirements

  • Complete sentences; "I agree" and "good point" do not count as replies.
  • Disagree with the idea, not the person.
  • Optional and ungraded: post any question about the play to Questions about the play.

Submit

  • Post in the All-Class Forum 1 discussion in Canvas: one initial post and replies to at least two classmates.

Done when

  • The first post takes a position in its first sentence.
  • A specific moment from the play or the tale is named.
  • The strongest objection to the position is answered.
  • A Module 6 vocabulary word is used correctly.

discussions.title: All-Class Forum 2 — What Lasts: Testing Your Claim
discussions.html:
PURPOSE: Test the claim planned for the "What Lasts" capstone by posting it for classmates to challenge.

Steps

  1. Name the theme (heroism, self-sacrifice, happiness, or duty) and three characters, each with their text.
  2. State the claim in one sentence: the actual argument about the theme, not "I am writing about duty." If it is not yet one sentence, post the best attempt.
  3. Name one specific scene from one of the three texts and say why it is the strongest evidence.
  4. Name the character who fits the claim worst and say what is awkward about that character.
  5. Reply to at least two classmates: test the fit of a character, test the claim with a counterexample from this year's reading, or solve a problem a classmate named.

Requirements

  • Replies stay hidden until the first post is submitted.
  • Complete sentences; "I agree" and "good point" do not count as replies.
  • Disagree with the idea, not the person.
  • Optional and ungraded: post any question about the year's reading to the questions thread.

Submit

  • Post in the All-Class Forum 2 discussion in Canvas: one initial post and replies to at least two classmates.

Done when

  • Theme and three characters are named with their texts.
  • The claim is one sentence and is the sentence planned for the essay.
  • One specific moment is named, with the reason it is the strongest evidence.
  • The least certain character is named, with what is awkward about them.
  • Two replies each test something or solve something.
